fields.title: Acquisition cost: how much you can pay for a customer
fields.keyTakeaway: The upper limit of customer cost is set by your unit economics, not the market: how much revenue they bring over their lifetime and how quickly they pay back the cost. Without these two numbers, talking about a "cheap" or "expensive" channel is meaningless.
fields.checkQuestion: A lead costs 800 ₽. What two numbers are missing to understand if it is cheap or expensive?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **how to acquire at a targeted cost?**
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **CAC** — total acquisition costs divided by the number of paying customers, not the number of leads.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **LTV** — how much revenue a paying customer brings over all time, minus service costs.
fields.blocks/1/items/2: **Payback period** — how many months it takes for a customer to pay back CAC. For a product without cash reserves, this number is more important than the LTV to CAC ratio.
fields.blocks/1/items/3: **Benchmark:** An LTV/CAC ratio around three is considered healthy, but it is a byproduct, not the goal; look at payback period and where the LTV forecast comes from.
fields.blocks/2/text:
Both yield leads at 800 ₽.

Search: 20% reach payment → CAC = 4 000 ₽. Average bill 1 200 ₽/mo, lifetime 14 months → LTV ≈ 16 800 ₽. Payback period — 3.3 months.

Social media: 3% reach payment → CAC = 26 700 ₽. Same 16 800 ₽ LTV. Channel is unprofitable, even though lead cost was identical.

Until conversion to payment is calculated, lead cost means nothing.
fields.blocks/2/title: Reestr, two channels with identical lead costs
fields.blocks/3/text: If a product is six months old, you don't know how long people stay: you only know they haven't left for six months. A cautious approach is to calculate actual LTV based on the observed timeframe and recalculate every quarter.
fields.blocks/3/title: LTV on a new product is a forecast, not a fact
fields.blocks/4/text: **What to do when a channel is expensive.** There are three levers, and you change them one at a time: lower touch cost (creative, bid), increase conversion to payment (offer, onboarding), or increase LTV (price, retention). The third is usually the strongest and the slowest.
fields.blocks/5/text: Averages across all customers hide distinct segments. It is helpful to calculate CAC and LTV separately by channel: often one channel holds all the profit while another burns through it, making everything look acceptable on average.
